title: Who Should Make That Decision?
author: Luca Foppoli
summary: Foppoli argues that decision rights in most organizations are settled by politics and hierarchy rather than by asking what kind of information a decision needs. He proposes an information gradient: breadth (information across products, departments and customers) rises with authority, while depth (information about a specific customer, market or problem) sits closer to the ground. The closer a decision is to the customer, the more depth should govern and the lower it should be made; the further away, the more breadth should govern. From this he derives a simple test, which is to delegate or escalate as soon as your own information is not deep or broad enough, and otherwise decide. He names three failure modes, overreach, abdication, and doing both at once, and illustrates each with a worked corporate scenario (a legal novation, a split marketing budget, a CRM rollout) showing what goes wrong and what the right division of decisions would look like. The practical takeaway is to ask what kind of information a decision needs before deciding who should make it.
points: Decision rights should follow an information gradient: breadth increases with seniority, depth increases with proximity to the customer, so the right decider is whoever holds the kind of information the decision requires.

Overreach, the person above deciding past the point where their information is relevant, is typically rooted in arrogance, turf wars or ignorance of others' viewpoints, and it produces damaged customer relationships and repair work below.

Abdication, never making the decision only the leader's breadth can make, leaves everyone below deciding blind; Foppoli's example is two products sharing one budget with no placement decision, so the company competes with itself.

The third failure mode combines the two: the leader decides what belongs below (fourteen mandatory CRM fields) and leaves undecided what only they can (what a qualified opportunity means), yielding a 50% completion rate on unusable data.

A practical test: if the decision needs more depth, delegate down; more breadth, escalate; if you already have enough of both, decide, and never let your job title fool you about which case you are in.
quotes: Decision rights are a non-topic in most organizations, with decisions made instead through politics and hierarchy. The problem is that the powerful step in on decisions for which they have the wrong kind of information.

When it comes to decision making, the closeness of the decision to the customer is the variable that should govern which kind of information is needed and therefore who should make the decision: the closer the decision is to the customer, the more depth should be used; the farther, the more breadth should govern.
The gradient comes with a simple test: you start delegating or escalating as soon as the information you have is not deep or broad enough for the decision that needs to be made.

When decision rights ignore the gradient, the result is a mess and extra work for everyone: decisions are made without the information they need or not made at all, while the people below spend their time cleaning up or deciding blind.

Overreach is when the person above keeps deciding past the point where his information stops being relevant. Arrogance, turf wars or plain ignorance of how the world looks from others’ points of view are the common root causes.
Abdication is when the person above never makes the decision only his breadth can make, leaving everyone below to decide blind. Cowardice or inadequacy for the role are the common root causes.
The budget is split for the company to compete with itself. Both products underperform.
After six months: leadership celebrates a 50% completion rate while the data are unusable, because “a qualified opportunity” means four different things in four different Countries.
context: Foppoli opens by naming the gap: most organizations never decide who decides, so hierarchy fills the vacuum.
This is the central rule of the piece, tying the level of a decision to the type of information it needs.
The gradient becomes a practical delegate, escalate or decide test a leader can apply to any decision.
He lists the costs of ignoring the gradient, which fall on the people below the decider.
The first failure mode is a senior person deciding things where their information has stopped being relevant.
The second failure mode is a leader declining the one decision only their breadth can make.
The marketing example shows abdication in numbers: one budget, two unprioritized products, both underperforming.
The CRM case shows the combined failure, where a metric looks healthy while the data underneath is unusable.
